8683.t: From Semitic, compare Hebrew גְּלוֹם (glōm, “wrap; mantle; cloak”), Late Babylonian 𒌆𒄖𒇷𒉡 (TUG₂.gu-li-nu /⁠gulīnu; gulēnu; gulānu⁠/, “over-cloak, coat”) likely a West-Semitic loan, Aramaic גְלִימָא (glīmā, “wrap; mantle; cloak”), whence also χλανίς…

8677.t: Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *gʰel(H)-ewH- (“tortoise, turtle-like animal”), and compared with Proto-Slavic *žely (“turtle, tortoise”); also related to χέλυς (khélus, “tortoise”).

8618.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally linked to a large group of words beginning with φλ- (phl-), like φλέω (phléō, “to overflow, abound”), φλύω (phlúō, “to be full of juice, thrive”), and φλύκταινα (phlúktaina, “blister”).

8617.t: Formally, it belongs to φλέω (phléō, “to abound”) together with φλόος (phlóos, “skin, slough”). Semantically, the connection with φλέω (phléō) is clear in ὑπέρφλοιος (hupérphloios, “luxuriant, succulent”).

8647.t: From φα(ν)- (phă(n)-, root of φαίνω (phaínō, “to bring to light; to appear”)) + -σις (-sĭs).

8659.t: The formation is similar to other bird names, like αἰγυπιός (aigupiós), αἰγωλιός (aigōliós) and ἐρῳδιός (erōidiós). Traditionally derived from χαράδρα (kharádra, “dry bed of a river”), but it could be folk etymology.

8651.t: Borrowed from a Semitic language, such as Hebrew פּוּךְ (pūk, “eye-rouge, antimony”).

8625.t: From φόνος (phónos), the o-grade of θείνω (theínō, “kill”), + -εύς (-eús, masculine agentive suffix).

8684.t: From the same Semitic root of χλαμύς (khlamús) and χλανίς (khlanís). Maybe also χλαμυρίς (khlamurís) and χλανίαι (khlaníai) are related.

8620.t: Perhaps a back-formation from φλυαρέω (phlŭāréō, “to talk nonsense”).

8668.t: Because of its basic meaning "loose, with holes, porous", is quite possible for this adjective to derive from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂-no-s, from *ǵʰeh₂- (“to yawn, hape”), like χάος (kháos, “abyss, chasm”), χαίνω (khaínō), and χάσκω (kháskō, “to gape,…

8615.t: From φιμός (phīmós, “any instrument for keeping the mouth closed”) + -όω (-óō, verbal suffix).

8629.t: From φόρτος (phórtos, “load, charge”) + -ίζω (-ĭ́zō, denominative verb suffix).
